entities.name: Pallava dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Pallava dynasty (275–897 CE) was a South Indian dynasty that ruled the region of Tondaimandalam (northern Tamil Nadu) from Kanchipuram, one of the sacred seven cities of Hinduism. The Pallavas were master builders and patrons of literature, creating the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and rock-cut monuments that became the prototype for Dravidian temple architecture across South and Southeast Asia.

The Pallavas reached their peak under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I (7th century CE), who defeated the Chalukyas in a series of wars. Narasimhavarman I earned the title 'Vatapi Kondan' (Conqueror of Vatapi) after sacking the Chalukya capital. The Mahabalipuram shore temple complex, built on the Bay of Bengal coast, includes the famous rathas (chariot temples) carved from single granite boulders, the Descent of the Ganges bas-relief (the world's largest open-air rock relief), and the Shore Temple — all UNESCO World Heritage sites.

The Pallavas are credited with developing the Grantha script from which Tamil, Malayalam, Sinhala, and several Southeast Asian scripts including Khmer, Javanese, and Thai scripts ultimately derive. The spread of Pallava-influenced architecture and Buddhism through trade networks shaped the temple traditions of Cambodia, Thailand, and Indonesia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Pallava dynasty's architectural and script innovations created Dravidian temple aesthetics and Southeast Asian writing systems, making Pallava cultural influence one of the most geographically extensive legacies in Asian history.
